title: Course Schedule
summary: prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means take b before a. Return whether all numCourses courses can be finished.
statement:
There are `numCourses` courses, numbered `0` to `numCourses − 1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prerequisites` means you must take course `b` before course `a`.

Return `true` if it is possible to finish every course.
hints: Courses are nodes and prerequisites are directed edges. When is finishing impossible?
It is impossible exactly when the graph has a cycle. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a course with no remaining prerequisites (in-degree 0) and remove its outgoing edges.
Count the courses you manage to take. If the count equals numCourses there is no cycle. (A DFS with three colours detects the cycle too.)
explain: The pair `[1,0]` means take course 0 before course 1. Take 0, then 1: both are finished, so the answer is `true`.

title: Course Schedule II
summary: Return any order in which all courses can be taken given the prerequisite pairs [a, b] (b first), or an empty array if impossible.
statement:
Same setup as "Course Schedule": `[a, b]` means course `b` must come before course `a`. Return an order in which you can take all `numCourses` courses.

If several orders work, return any of them. If it is impossible, return an empty array.
hints: An order that respects every prerequisite is a topological order of the graph.
Run Kahn's algorithm and append each course to the answer when you take it from the queue.
If the answer ends up shorter than numCourses, the graph has a cycle: return an empty array.
explain: Course 0 has no prerequisite and course 1 needs course 0, so the only valid order is `[0,1]`.

title: Course Schedule IV
summary: Given direct prerequisites [a, b] (a before b), answer each query [u, v]: is u a prerequisite of v, directly or indirectly?
statement:
Courses are numbered `0` to `numCourses − 1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prerequisites` means course `a` must be taken before course `b` (note the direction is the opposite of "Course Schedule"). Prerequisites can be indirect: if `a` comes before `b` and `b` before `c`, then `a` is a prerequisite of `c`.

For each query `[u, v]`, answer whether `u` is a prerequisite of `v`. The prerequisite graph has no cycles.
hints: There are many queries but at most 100 courses, so precompute every reachability answer once.
Build a boolean reach[u][v] table. Either run a DFS/BFS from every course, or use Floyd–Warshall style: reach[i][j] |= reach[i][k] && reach[k][j].
Then every query is a single table lookup.
explain: Here `[1,0]` means course 1 comes before course 0. So 0 is not a prerequisite of 1, while 1 is a prerequisite of 0, giving `[false,true]`.

title: Minimum Height Trees
summary: An undirected tree has n nodes. Return every node that, used as the root, gives the minimum possible height. Any order.
statement:
An undirected tree has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1` and the given `edges`. Choosing any node as the root gives a rooted tree with some height (the number of edges on its longest root-to-leaf path).

Return every node that, chosen as the root, gives the minimum possible height. The order does not matter.
hints: Running a BFS from every node to measure heights is O(n²).
The best roots are in the "middle" of the longest path. Peel the tree from the outside in: remove all current leaves, then the new leaves, and so on.
Track degrees and remove leaves level by level, like a topological sort. When at most two nodes remain, they are the answer.
explain: Node 1 is joined to every other node, so rooting the tree at 1 gives height 1. Rooting at any leaf gives height 2, so the only answer is `[1]`.

title: Find Eventual Safe States
summary: In a directed graph (graph[i] lists i's targets), a node is safe if every path from it ends at a node with no outgoing edges. Return all safe nodes in ascending order.

perf.label: 10,000 nodes
perf.gen: int n = 10000; int[][] a0 = new int[n][]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { TreeSet<Integer> ts = new TreeSet<>(); int deg = BCB.rnd(0, 4); while (ts.size() < deg) ts.add(BCB.rnd(0, n - 1)); a0[i] = ts.stream().mapToInt(x -> x).toArray(); }

statement:
`graph` is a directed graph: `graph[i]` lists the nodes that node `i` has edges to. A terminal node has no outgoing edges. A node is safe if every path starting from it leads to a terminal node (so it can never get stuck in a cycle).

Return all safe nodes in ascending order.
constraints: `graph[i]` is sorted and has no duplicates
hints: A node is unsafe exactly when it can reach a cycle.
Reverse every edge. Terminal nodes are safe; a node becomes safe once all its original successors are safe. That is Kahn's algorithm on the reversed graph, starting from the terminal nodes.
Alternatively, DFS with three colours (unvisited, in progress, safe): a node that reaches an "in progress" node is on or leads to a cycle.
explain: Nodes 5 and 6 have no outgoing edges, and 2 and 4 only lead to 5, so they are safe. Nodes 0, 1 and 3 can loop forever through 0 → 1 → 3 → 0, so the answer is `[2,4,5,6]`.

title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
summary: Recipe i needs every item in ingredients[i]; ingredients can be supplies (unlimited) or other recipes. Return every recipe you can make, in any order.
statement:
You have the recipes in `recipes`; recipe `i` needs every item in `ingredients[i]`. An ingredient can be one of your `supplies` (of which you have an unlimited amount) or another recipe that you must make first.

Return every recipe you can make, in any order.
constraints: All names are lowercase, 1 to 10 characters, and recipe names do not repeat
hints: A recipe can be made once all of its ingredients are available. Recipes that depend on each other in a loop can never be made.
Topological sort: the in-degree of a recipe is the number of its ingredients. Start a queue with all supplies.
When an item becomes available, decrement every recipe that uses it. A recipe reaching 0 is made, and joins the queue as a new available item.
explain: Bread needs yeast and flour, and both are in the supplies, so bread can be made. The answer is `["bread"]`.

title: Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies
summary: Order n items so that items of the same group are next to each other and every item comes after all items in beforeItems[i]. group[i] = -1 means no group. Return any valid order, or [] if none exists.
statement:
There are `n` items. `group[i]` is the group of item `i` (`0` to `m − 1`), or `-1` if it belongs to no group. `beforeItems[i]` lists the items that must come before item `i`.

Return an ordering of all items such that items of the same group are next to each other, and every item comes after all of its `beforeItems`. If several orderings work, return any. If none exists, return an empty array.
constraints: beforeItems[i] has no duplicates and does not contain i
hints: There are two layers of ordering: groups relative to each other, and items inside each group.
Give every ungrouped item its own new group. Then build two graphs: one between groups (from dependencies that cross groups) and one between items.
Topologically sort both graphs. If either has a cycle, return []. Then output the groups in their sorted order, and within each group its items in their sorted order.
explain: Group 0 holds items 3, 4 and 6, and group 1 holds items 2 and 5. In `[6,3,4,5,2,0,7,1]` each group's items sit together, 6 comes before 1, 3 and 4, 3 comes before 4, and 5 comes before 2, so every rule holds. Other orders that satisfy the rules are also accepted.
